title: Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG
gist: Uber's Legal Redlining Agent, a Microsoft Word add-in combining RAG over playbooks and historical lawyer feedback with a deterministic rules engine, cut average contract review time by more than 20% with 91% decision accuracy, while lawyers keep approval authority.

insights.claim: Uber's Legal Redlining Agent reduced average contract review time by more than 20% with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, with lawyers retaining responsibility for approving recommendations.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete enterprise ROI benchmark for legal AI copilots; ~20% time savings with human-in-the-loop is a realistic bar for legal-tech vendors.

insights.claim: Uber's agent runs inside Microsoft Word, identifying counterparty edits, interpreting intent, comparing them to legal policy and recommending accept/reject/modify with explanatory comments; development began in early 2024 with a Legal team pilot in 2025.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Large enterprises are building in-house legal AI on general-purpose stacks rather than buying, a competitive threat to specialized legal-tech vendors.

themes.theme: Why naive RAG failed and feedback fixed it

insights.claim: Uber's initial RAG over legal playbooks struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone and uncovered scenarios, which led it to add a feedback loop capturing lawyers' decisions, reasoning and final edited text.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Playbook-only RAG is insufficient for judgment-heavy domains; proprietary expert-feedback data is the real moat for vertical AI.

insights.claim: At runtime Uber narrows thousands of historical lawyer interactions to about 20 candidates via similarity search and metadata filtering, then applies a second LLM-based relevance filter and exponential decay weighting with a 365-day half-life.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable retrieval pattern (two-stage filter plus recency decay) for enterprise agents built on institutional precedent.

insights.claim: A deterministic rules engine enforces Uber's non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a rule matches, while LLMs handle contextual interpretation and tone, followed by a final verification against retrieved rules.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Rules-over-LLM guardrails are emerging as the standard pattern for regulated/high-stakes AI deployments.

insights.claim: Uber's stack combines a React/TypeScript Word add-in, a Python backend orchestrated by LangGraph with parallel nodes for intent detection, risk assessment and policy lookup, OpenSearch for vectorized rules and feedback, and Redis for session state.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: LangGraph and OpenSearch gaining production enterprise agent deployments signals their ecosystem traction.

insights.claim: Uber's legal team defines tone and style while engineers maintain the prompt structure and workflow, splitting ownership between domain experts and engineering.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Domain-expert control over prompts is an adoption enabler for AI in professional services.
insights.quote: How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?
insights.locator: The legal team defines the desired tone

insights.claim: Uber is exploring agentic harnesses including Claude Code and OpenCode, with skills to structure workflows, and plans to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs for more consistent reasoning.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: General coding-agent harnesses are being repurposed for non-coding enterprise workflows, expanding the addressable market for agent platforms like Anthropic's.
insights.locator: Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses
